rv.q: The actor inhabits Rothko completely, giving one of those unnerving performances that makes you believe in the possibility of reincarnation.
For 90 largely plotless minutes, theatergoers are riveted to this play, unable to extricate themselves from both the performances and the show itself.
As forcefully delivered in Molina’s volcanic performance, this torrent of observations is consistently engrossing.
Alfred Molina is majestic as Rothko, defying the future he reads in the face of Eddie Redmayne, who holds his own as Rothko’s young assistant.
Molina, an actor in constant demand on both sides of the pond, plays Rothko at full titanic force.
What we see, above all, is an artist seeing, and it’s impossible not to feel thrilled by the privilege.
The success of Logan’s smart, eloquent entertainment is to bring us in there with him.

There's a little too much talk of how paintings 'pulse' and a few of the assistant's background details seem unnecessarily maudlin. No doubt these were inserted to give his character depth, so he'd be more than just Rothko's sounding board. While the role may not be as well-drawn as Rothko's, Redmayne certainly knows what to do with it.
The shifting dynamics in this brutally honest portrait of the artist make for the most intellectually stimulating 90 minutes Broadway has seen in years.
"Red" is a compelling example of how a thinking theater can simultaneously entertain and educate.
There's barely a cliché left unturned in John Logan's 'Red,' a two-hander about the late-in-life creative struggles of artist Mark Rothko, arriving direct from London's Donmar Warehouse.
It turns out to be an engrossing look at Abstract Expressionist painter Mark Rothko.

cn.t: Logan's intellectually stimulating portrait of Mark Rothko divides critics. Most praise Molina's commanding performance and the play's electrifying debate on art, though some find it clichéd and more talk than drama.

vs.sum: The John Golden Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, though sound quality can vary, especially under the mezzanine. Seating comfort is typical of older theaters with tight legroom, but the venue maintains a pleasant ambiance overall. Facilities are adequate, though not exceptional.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No wheelchair-accessible restroom (use adjacent Schoenfeld).
